newsitem.title: UK: Aluminium prices drop, by almost 25 pct since Jan.
newsitem.headline: Aluminium prices drop, by almost 25 pct since Jan.

text.p: Aluminium prices fell to their lowest for 2-1/2 years on Thursday, driven down by rising stocks, bank and technical selling and lack of any significant consumer buying interest.
The metal which is used in packaging, canning and transportation has lost nearly a quarter of its value since the first trading day of 1996.
On the London Metal Exchange (LME) three month futures slumped to $1,305 a tonne on Thursday from $1,323 at the close on Wednesday, before bouncing to $1,318 by midday.
The market opened the year at $1,700 on January 2.
"There has been some heavy selling out of the U.S. recently," said Macquarie Equities analyst Adam Rowley, responding to floor trader talk of selling from U.S. banks.
"But the other side is that for a long while now the consumers have been sitting back from the market," he added.

"The market continues to be dragged lower as consumer demand remains weak and producer/option-related selling keep stalling any signs of recovery," said Christopher Hill of LME ring dealers the Gerald Group.
Consumer demand throughout the year has fallen well short of expectations because buyers drew on their own stocks. This phase is thought to be close to completion, according to analysts.

Producer stocks rose in August, reflecting slow metal demand. On Thursday the International Primary Aluminium Institute (IPAI) estimated total producer stocks at 3.347 million tonnes at the end of August from 3.342 million in July.
Over the year the total has fallen from 3.701 million tonnes at the end of January.
But while consumer and producer stocks dwindled, the more visible LME stockpile swelled, helping to depress values. Stocks stand at 967,825 tonnes from 584,425 at the start of the year.
Also weighing on the market are "hidden" stocks held in non-LME warehouses and financed by banks.
J.P Morgan's Kevin Crisp on Monday estimated unreported stocks tied up in financing deals at 500,000 to 600,000 tonnes, although some analysts said this figure may be slightly high.
Despite aluminium's woeful performance this week, traders and analysts gathered in London for the annual LME banquet were mostly bullish in the long term.
"We think the tide for aluminium is already turning," Morgan's Crisp told an LME metals seminar on Monday.
He forecast an average price next year of $1,680 from $1,524 in 1996 - a rise of 10 percent.
The more positive outlook for the market is based on hopes of rising demand and the end of the de-stocking phase.
"Next year we could start to see demand coming back, and when it does it could surprise people by how strong it is," said Macquarie's Rowley.
Physical traders and producers have also seen a modest pick-up in orders suggesting a price recovery soon.
"Demand and premiums are hardening, and I am facing shortages in delivering," David Reuben, head of major trade group Trans-world Metals said in an interview last week.
However, in the short term the market is vulnerable.
"The real danger now is that prices break down below the $1,300 level and head towards $1,250 and possibly lower," brokers Brandeis said in a report.
